details:
What it does

FireCalendar turns 23 years of NASA FIRMS fire hotspots into a burning calendar for any place on Earth. Pick a country, draw an area or type coordinates, and see every month since 2003 in one grid, each month compared with its usual level, a weekly forecast and a 3-month outlook. You can download the hotspots as CSV and a PDF report. A chat assistant answers plain-language questions from the same data and cites its sources.

How it works

MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) see fire differently: VIIRS finds 3–4 times as many hotspots, so the raw record jumps in 2012 though nothing changed on the ground. We put both on one scale, VIIRS S-NPP. MODIS months up to January 2012 are converted to what VIIRS would have seen, with models learned region by region where both satellites flew (2012–2020). From February 2012 the record is observed VIIRS, and since S-NPP stopped in November 2026, NOAA-20 carries it on. On years the models never saw, monthly error is 3.8–14.7% across 14 world regions, and low, normal and high months agree 61–92% of the time. The result is 408 million hotspots in 0.25° cells, month by month; where a model never trained, error rises to 8–27%, and the site says so.

Forecasts are shown only where they beat the usual level. A week ahead, the world-total forecast misses by 13.9%, against 17.0% for the usual level, and its 80% ranges held 80% of the time. A month ahead, the 3-month outlook misses by 10.2%, against 13.3%, and beats the usual pattern in 14 of 15 regions.

Benefits and impact

Trends, "normal" months and alerts built on the raw record are wrong. In Argentina, burning looks 128% higher in 2012–20 than in 2003–11 as recorded; on one scale it fell 25%. FireCalendar gives emergency responders a fair answer to "is now unusual, and what comes next?", land managers the timing of the season and its worst months, and scientists one consistent record since 2003, with its uncertainty and methods.

Tools

Python for the data pipeline and models (XGBoost; PyTorch RNN, LSTM and GRU; climatology and Markov baselines; ensembles), trained on a GPU when available. FastAPI and DuckDB for the data API. Next.js and TypeScript for the website, with MapLibre and deck.gl for the map and ECharts for the charts. The chat assistant uses Groq's API: a first model checks that the question is about fire, and a second answers by calling our own endpoints, so every number is one the site shows. The key stays on the server. Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1; VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21), plus NOAA CPC soil moisture, GPCP precipitation, GHCN-CAMS temperature, ONI (El Niño) and DMI (Indian Ocean Dipole) for the outlook.

What makes it creative

The burning calendar shows two decades of fire at a glance, with unusually high months outlined. Forecasts appear only where they beat the usual, so the site never shows a forecast it can't back up. We also checked sensor continuity: the drift in Terra's and Aqua's overpass times, a model of fire through the day, and a scorecard of our conversion against S-NPP from 2012 to 2026.

What we considered

Honest uncertainty (every error measured on years the models never saw), the end of S-NPP, differences between regions, orbit drift, use on phone and desktop, accessible color scales, and keeping keys out of the browser.
